summary: If you’ve ever tried adding an AI feature to an app, you know that you should set up a server, figure out GPU hosting, and spend half your week reading infrastructure docs. Cloud providers finally realized nobody wants to do that. Let's get acquainted with Amazon Bedrock. Instead of managing servers, you get a single API endpoint that connects to hundreds of foundation models, like Claude, Llama, Nova, Mistral, and more. No infrastructure: No servers or GPUs to configure. Pay-per-token. You pay only for what you use. Prompts and responses are not used to train models and are not shared with providers. Inside you can find lists of over 200 serverless and marketplace models. You can filter by provider (Amazon Nova, Anthropic Claude, Meta Llama, etc.) to check parameters and capabilities. Playground lets you test prompts in your browser before writing code. Pick a lightweight option like Amazon Nova 2 Light, give it a system prompt, and run a quick test. Some models (like Meta Llama) have regional restrictions or licensing limits. Providers like Anthropic require a one-time use-case form per account (company name, website, industry, and use-case description) before granting model access. Bedrock uses the Converse API, providing a uniform request structure across all models. The payload requires three main fields: modelId , messages , inferenceConfig . import boto3 from config import REGION , MODEL_ID bedrock = boto3 . client ( " bedrock-runtime " , region_name = REGION ) start =
title: Stop Managing GPUs. Use the AWS Bedrock Converse API - One Python API, Hundreds of LLMs

summary: TL;DR A team of 5 ran 986 reviews over about 10 weeks on a single CDK infrastructure repository. Each review took about 60 seconds on average, and the actual Bedrock bill totaled $180.60 (about $0.18 per review) Review count, cost, and duration are now visible as numbers, but we still can't measure whether the findings were correct, or how lead time changed before and after adoption Table of Contents Introduction Architecture Overview How the PR Review Works Measuring the Effect Visualization Thinking About Cost Results in Production Design Decisions Limitations and Future Improvements Conclusion Introduction CodeCommit is a very convenient service that lets you keep your whole development environment inside AWS. However, compared with GitHub, its surrounding ecosystem is limited. An OSS tool such as Qodo AI's PR-Agent has a provider for CodeCommit, but its features are limited and it assumes you use it from the CLI. So I built a mechanism that reviews CodeCommit pull requests (PRs) with Amazon Bedrock and posts the result as comments. I did not use the OSS PR-Agent. Instead, I built it from scratch with EventBridge and Lambda so that it runs automatically whenever a PR is created or updated. Many of the articles I referred to ended at "post the comment", but once you think about operating it, you also need to make the following visible: How much does it cost per month? Whose PRs are they, and how many tokens does each model use? Are findings actually being raised, and if so,
title: Automating CodeCommit PR Reviews with Amazon Bedrock: 986 Reviews in 10 Weeks, $0.18 Each, and What We Could Not Measure

summary: This article provides a step by step guide to measuring Gemma 4 E2B's speed and accuracy at every quantization rung a second time, on an NVIDIA L4 in AWS, with the same nine GGUF files and the same llama.cpp build as the Tesla T4 run, and comparing the two GPUs question by question. https://github.com/xbill9/gemma-graveyard The first article quantized Gemma 4 E2B from BF16 to Q2_K on one Tesla T4, asked every rung the same 250 GSM8K questions, and recorded each answer's grade at every rung. This one moves the whole ladder to a g6.xlarge . The nine files have the same sha256 on both machines, both run llama.cpp b11699 , and each machine gives identical text when a rung is run twice. The GPU changes, and with it the driver, the CUDA version and the kernels that do the arithmetic. The Results in Brief The L4 decodes every rung faster than the T4, from 1.25 times at BF16 to 1.89 times at Q2_K, and Q5_K_M stays the best trade between speed and accuracy: 228 right against BF16's 229, at 2.15 times BF16's decode speed on the L4. The grades move with the GPU. With the same file and the same build, the L4 and the T4 grade 2 questions differently at BF16, 7 at Q5_K_M, 16 at Q4_0 and 33 at Q3_K_M. At Q5_K_M that is nearly the whole quantization effect on the T4, where Q5_K_M against BF16 was 8 questions: 3 lost and 5 gained. Of the 226 questions lost at some rung on each GPU, 180 are first lost at the same rung on both. The cover lays the two GPUs' grades over each other. One row per ru
title: Performance vs Quality: Gemma 4 E2B Quantization on an NVIDIA L4 and a Tesla T4

summary: Black Friday peak. The checkout has microservices, a CI/CD pipeline, containers, serverless functions, every piece with its own deploy and a green dashboard. Then the settlement service, way at the end of the chain, starts responding slowly, and within minutes the whole payment authorization flow is timing out. On paper, every service was independent. The customer still gave up on the purchase while waiting for the approval. That scene has a name, invisible coupling, and so does the system it produces: a distributed monolith. If this sounds familiar, stick with me, this post is for you. It kicks off a short run of posts on the topic: next I'll show how to break these dependencies by separating the hot path from the side-effects, walk through the patterns that hold that split together, and wrap up hands-on with a prototype on AWS. Validity note: written in October 2026. The argument here is about architecture and doesn't expire with a release, but the AWS links (Well-Architected, Builders' Library) get reorganized from time to time. If one of them points somewhere odd, let me know in the comments and I'll fix it. Invisible coupling: what a distributed monolith really is Coupling is a measure of how much one service depends on another to work. My provocation, right up front: if your microservice only responds because another one responded first, that independence is an illusion. In practice, it's part of a distributed monolith. Sam Newman explores that term, distributed monolit
title: Invisible Coupling: When Your Microservices Become a Distributed Monolith

summary: Changing the runtime and the access path without moving the data: how authentication, authorization, and failures differ A long-lived business application often keeps the data it reads and writes on a file share. For rebuilding such an application on a newer language or runtime, Microsoft Learn lists dependencies reaching end of support, new security or compliance requirements, and performance or scalability limits as the signals ( Upgrade .NET apps overview ). Its examples include moving a Windows-only .NET Framework app to cross-platform modern .NET, and beyond that, containerizing the app or replacing components with managed services. When you rebuild an application, what usually stalls the effort is not the application itself but what to do with the data it has been reading and writing. Moving the data to a new store brings along downtime during the migration, redesigning permissions, re-pointing reference paths, and re-validating on the destination. This bundle is what stops modernization. Not moving the data removes that whole bundle, because it decouples rebuilding the app from migrating the data. You get three things: You avoid the migration work itself. No downtime, no permission redesign, no path re-pointing, no destination re-validation. You can focus only on changing the app's language or runtime. The data stays a single source of truth that several runtimes share at once. No extra copies to keep in sync. summary: When a Kubernetes cluster runs out of room, something has to add nodes. For years that job belonged to the Cluster Autoscaler, which scales fixed-size node groups up and down. Karpenter takes a different approach: it looks at the pods that can't be scheduled, works out the cheapest mix of instances that would fit them, and launches those instances directly. No pre-defined node groups to size, no guessing which instance type to standardise on. In this post we build an EKS cluster with Terraform, install Karpenter, and prove the scaling works by pushing a real Node.js app up and down. Every snippet comes straight from the repo linked at the end. What we are building The stack splits cleanly into two layers: Terraform stands up the VPC, the EKS control plane, a small managed node group to host system pods and the Karpenter controller, and all the IAM / SQS plumbing Karpenter needs. summary: An agent that behaved correctly on launch day is silently making bad decisions two months later. Nobody changed the code; the world it judges just drifted away from the prompt it was given. This use case builds that failure on purpose: an expense-audit agent whose system prompt carries one stale sentence, then walks the full quality loop Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides — observe the spans, evaluate the traces, cluster the failures, optimize the prompt, ship the fix as a configuration bundle, and prove it with an A/B test and a CI gate. Every number below was measured in one account, us-east-1 . The use case The travel desk at Northwind Gear runs an expense auditor: a receipt goes in, a reimbursement decision comes out. Finance does not complain that it crashes — they complain that international hotel bills keep coming back approved at suspiciously round numbers, and nobody can say which of the two-month-old instructions is to blame. What AgentCore does here Four capabilities carry the loop. Runtime: hosts the Strands agent and streams its decisions; the prompt it runs comes from a configuration bundle, not from the code. Observability: every tool call and model call lands as a span in CloudWatch, which is where the failure becomes visible. Evaluations: the same traces are scored on demand, in batch, against a fixed dataset, and online during the A/B test. Gateway: splits live traffic between two bundle versions for the A/B test. summary: This article provides a step by step guide to building an hourly transit reach map with Amazon Location Service. Walking areas come from Pedestrian isolines, journey times come from Transit routing, and the finished map runs as static files on Amazon S3 and Amazon CloudFront. A transit desert is a place where demand for transit outruns the service on offer. Published maps usually score that gap once per area. Service changes by the hour, so this project scores it for every hour of a weekday. The study area is Mercer County, New Jersey. It holds Trenton, Princeton and a ring of suburbs, and 16,114 of its 144,114 households have no car. summary: __ Level 300 — Advanced | Amazon EKS, Argo CD, AWS DevOps Agent, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Kiro CLI, Amazon EventBridge 🎯 The Challenge Scenario Suppose you are the Platform Engineering lead of an enterprise that already runs Kubernetes the GitOps way: an Amazon EKS hub cluster with Argo CD manages a fleet of spoke clusters , and every team onboards its workloads through a single values file in Git. It works. Deployments are boring, in a good way. Operations are not. On-call engineers keep getting paged for the same kind of incidents: a bad config is merged, pods start crash-looping, and someone spends 40 minutes reading logs and events before realizing the fix is "revert that commit". Then leadership asks the question every platform team is hearing: "Can AI agents take the first part of on-call?" Your mission: add agentic investigation and remediation to the existing platform , under these constraints: ✅ No agent gets write access to production. Not to the cluster, not to the AWS account. ✅ Every fix is a reviewable pull request. Git stays the single source of truth; Argo CD stays the only thing that changes the cluster. ✅ Don't rebuild the platform. The hub-spoke GitOps setup stays as it is; agents are added on top. ✅ Multi-account by design. Workloads and CI/CD live in different AWS accounts. ✅ Everything is observable and auditable. Every agent action leaves a trace. This post is the architecture behind the TechLabVel video, Cap 2 . My Approach: Eyes, Not Hands The fastes
title: Eyes, Not Hands: Adding AWS DevOps Agent, Bedrock AgentCore and Kiro to a GitOps Platform on EKS

summary: This article provides a step by step guide to finding drift in an agent skill and closing it with a repeatable feedback loop. The working example is publishing-kit, an agent skill for Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity that publishes one markdown article to five destinations. https://github.com/xbill9/publishing-kit A skill is a set of claims about a world that keeps moving. Every claim has a shelf life, so maintenance is a loop you run on a schedule. What Is Skill Drift? A skill is instructions plus scripts, and both describe something outside the skill: an editor, an API, a file format, or another script. Drift is the distance between what the skill says and what is true today. It grows without any error message, because the skill keeps loading and its checks keep passing. Why Does a Green Check Prove So Little? The kit runs a pre-flight against its own article. On the day of this audit that run exited 0: $ python3 skills/publishing/scripts/preflight.py articles/publishing-kit-skill/devto-publishing-kit.md --live all checks passed The same day, a code review of the scripts returned 20 findings and running every generator by hand added 2 more. One of those unpublished live articles. The pre-flight walks a happy path. An article that never contains a ~~~ block can never show that 8 files mishandle one. title: Agent Skills Drift: A Feedback Loop for Keeping One True
